title: An ideal-power torsion module has a presentation by cyclic ideal-power quotients
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq R$ an ideal and $Q$ an $R$-module such that every $q\in Q$ is annihilated by $I^n$ for some $n\ge1$. There are a set $J$, positive integers $n_j$ for $j\in J$, the $R$-module $P=\bigoplus_{j\in J}R/I^{n_j}$ [def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules] of the quotient modules $R/I^{n_j}$ [def-weil-pbc-quotient-module], and a surjective $R$-linear map $p:P\to Q$. Its kernel $K$ is itself $I$-power torsion: every $k\in K$ is annihilated by $I^n$ for some $n\ge1$. Consequently $0\to K\to P\xrightarrow{p}Q\to0$, with $K\to P$ the inclusion, is a short exact sequence of $R$-modules [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence].

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E8 (lemma-I-power-torsion-presentation, line 24002), first step of its proof

proof.text: Take $J=Q$ as index set. For $q\in Q$ let $n_q$ be the smallest integer $n\ge1$ with $I^nq=0$, which exists by hypothesis (for $q=0$, $n_q=1$). Define $\varphi_q:R/I^{n_q}\to Q$ by $\varphi_q(r+I^{n_q})=rq$. It is well defined: if $r-r'\in I^{n_q}$ then $(r-r')q=0$ because $I^{n_q}q=0$ means that every element of $I^{n_q}$ kills $q$. It is $R$-linear since $(r+I^{n_q})+(r'+I^{n_q})=(r+r')+I^{n_q}$ and $s(r+I^{n_q})=sr+I^{n_q}$ [def-weil-pbc-quotient-module], and $\varphi_q(1+I^{n_q})=q$. In Lean, use Nat.find on the torsion hypothesis and lift LinearMap.toSpanSingleton through Submodule.liftQ.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E8 (lemma-I-power-torsion-presentation), proof, first two sentences

proof.text: Put $P=\bigoplus_{q\in Q}R/I^{n_q}$ [def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules] and define $p:P\to Q$ by $p((x_q)_q)=\sum_{q}\varphi_q(x_q)$; the sum is finite because $x_q=0$ for all but finitely many $q$, and $p$ is $R$-linear because addition and scalar multiplication in $P$ are componentwise and each $\varphi_q$ is $R$-linear (step 1). Then $p\circ\iota_q=\varphi_q$ for the canonical inclusion $\iota_q$, so $p(\iota_q(1+I^{n_q}))=q$ for every $q\in Q$ and $p$ is surjective. This is the canonical surjection $\bigoplus_{m\in M}R/I^{n_m}\to M\to0$ of the source. In Lean, DirectSum.toModule assembles these maps; DirectSum.toModule_lof evaluates it on each summand.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E8 (lemma-I-power-torsion-presentation), proof, first two sentences

proof.text: Prove that every element of P is annihilated by a positive power of I by DirectSum.induction_on [def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules]. Zero is annihilated by I^1. For a single summand R/I^{n_q}, lift its element to r in R through Submodule.mkQ_surjective [def-weil-pbc-quotient-module]; for a in I^{n_q}, ar belongs to I^{n_q}, so its class is zero. The inclusion of that summand is linear, so the corresponding element of P is killed too. If x and y are annihilated by I^m and I^l, respectively, then m>0 implies max(m,l)>0, and Ideal.pow_le_pow_right gives I^{max(m,l)} contained in both I^m and I^l. Scalar multiplication distributes over addition, so this power kills x+y. Finally apply this result to the underlying element of each k in ker(p), and use subtype extensionality to obtain the equality in the kernel.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E8 (lemma-I-power-torsion-presentation), proof, first two sentences

proof.text: Apply Mathlib's LinearMap.shortExact_shortComplexKer to the surjectivity proved in step 2. This gives precisely p.shortComplexKer.ShortExact [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]: its first map is the kernel inclusion, its second map is p, and the lemma supplies exactness, monicity of the inclusion and epimorphicity of p. No Grothendieck-category assertion is needed.

split_report.summary: Read Stacks More on Algebra 05E8 (more-algebra-lemma-I-power-torsion-presentation, tag verified in tags/tags) and its proof; the item is its first two sentences. Split into four elementary steps following the proof: the maps R/I^{n_q}->Q, 1->q (well defined because I^{n_q}q=0), the canonical surjection from the direct sum over Q, the I-power torsion of P (finite support, I^{max n_q}) and hence of the kernel, and the short exact sequence in Mod(R).
